title: The grain of wheat (John 12:24)
hookLine: unless the grain falls and dies, it stays alone

lines: SOME GREEKS ASK TO SEE HIM.
cards: A packet of seeds can sit in a kitchen drawer for years. Open it, and the seeds are all still there, a bit drier. Nothing has gone wrong, exactly.
Nothing has happened at all. Put one in the dirt, and it stops being a seed. It splits, it disappears into roots and a stalk, and if you're lucky, a whole head of grain.
Jesus is in Jerusalem now, with the Passover close, and some Greeks have come asking to see him. His answer is about a seed.

teach.b: Some Greeks, Gentiles in the Douay, people who had come up to worship at the feast, find Philip: Sir, we would see Jesus. Philip tells Andrew, and the two of them tell Jesus. Then Jesus says the hour has come.
All through John, his hour has been not yet; at Cana, my hour is not yet come. Now, when outsiders arrive wanting to see him, the hour is here.

teach.h: UNLESS IT DIE, IT STAYS ALONE.
teach.b: And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Notice the word alone.
The opposite of bearing fruit, here, isn't failure. It's staying alone, intact and unchanged. A grain that keeps itself is safe, and it's by itself forever.
Jesus is talking first about his own death. Readers hear an answer to the Greeks in it: a few lines on he says, if I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.

Then he widens it: he that loveth his life shall lose it, and he that hateth his life in this world keepeth it unto life eternal. Some readers hear hate there as a strong Semitic way of saying, don't cling.
Early Christians took the seed picture straight to the martyrs.

teach.h: THE BLOOD OF CHRISTIANS IS SEED.
teach.b: Tertullian wrote that the blood of Christians is seed: the more they're cut down, the more they grow.
Catholics also hear it in smaller deaths: a pride let go, a grudge buried, an evening given up.

how: The Church reads John 12:20–33 on the Fifth Sunday of Lent in Year B, and on the feast of Saint Lawrence, deacon and martyr.

games.q: what does “the grain of wheat” mean?
o: the first fruits offered in the temple
a death that leads to much new life
a reward saved up for the harvest

p: my hour is not yet come
the blood of Christians is seed

s: in this saying, the opposite of bearing fruit is staying alone
unless it die, itself remaineth alone.
Jesus says the hour has come right after Greeks ask to see him
John 12:20–23: outsiders arrive, and the hour is here.
hateth his life means Jesus wants people to despise themselves
some readers hear it as a strong way of saying don't cling.

games.q: you're Philip. some Greeks visiting Jerusalem for the feast come to you and say, sir, we would see Jesus. what do you do?
o: tell them he only speaks to Jews.
go and tell Andrew, and the two of you tell Jesus.
bring them straight into the crowd.
games.why: Philip tells Andrew and they tell Jesus together. his answer is that the hour has come, and the grain must fall.

practice: Open your hands on your lap and breathe, and find one small self-interest from today: needing to win an argument, the last word, the bigger slice, the credit. Picture it leaving your hands and going into the ground.
If you pray, hold the line, if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit; if not, keep your hands open and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The grain of wheat. Jesus's picture of his own death: a seed that stays alone unless it falls, and bears much fruit when it does. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: falls and bears fruit. The grain falls, and the field comes later. Day five hundred fifteen, done.
